reason: The court dealt only with a transferee of a contingent post-lis-pendens interest, so the statement is overbroad despite being drawn from the holding.
The court rejected the proposition that this contingent transferee had an interest in the land under section 69, rather than affirming it.
The judgment expressly held that contingent interest was not included in the relevant phrase, making the extracted statement the opposite of the holding.
The rule misstates the provision as section 5.408 and omits that the remedy was to the Court of Appeal by revision or restitutio in integrum.
The statement drops the writ-pending-appeal and substantial-loss context in which absence of loss material favoured the plaintiff-respondent.
The court treated substantiality of the legal question as dependent on the facts of the case when refusing to stay writ.
The court applied the principle that a prospective purchaser in possession is only a licensee or permissive occupier, not a tenant.
The statement omits the important qualification that revision is discretionary and exercised to correct illegality or prevent miscarriage of justice.
The court held that a defendant seeking to partition a larger land must comply with the Partition Law procedure including sections 4, 5, and 6.
The court held that registering lis pendens alone was insufficient without following the full larger-land procedure in section 19(2).
The court relied on section 70 and actus curiae to hold that the court had to compel prosecution and parties should not suffer from court-caused delay.
The court construed section 16 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance as requiring due duplicate attestation of deeds.
The wording is materially imprecise because the defect was not corrections on a copy as such, but non-matching and unattested corrections across duplicate copies.
The court rejected the argument that the duplicate could be treated as a draft under the Notaries Ordinance.
This is a general policy observation about contempt jurisdiction, not the holding needed to decide liability.
The court held that contempt is criminal in character and must be proved beyond reasonable doubt before finding guilt.
The judgment distinguished injunction cases and held that Sri Lankan law does not strictly require proof of wilful mens rea for disobedience of an injunction.
The court used the Mortgage Act's substantive and procedural role while holding the commercial mortgage action fell within Commercial High Court jurisdiction.
The statement is too vague and omits the High Court of the Provinces Act, commercial-transaction threshold, and jurisdictional context.
The condition-precedent point concerned the Conciliation Board Act only as a contrast, while the case turned on the absolute bar in section 56 of the Debt Conciliation Ordinance.
The extracted statement generalizes all jurisdictional defects, whereas the court held only that the section 56 Debt Conciliation Ordinance bar was patent on these facts.
The passage is a fact-specific finding about the defendant priest's conduct, not a legal ratio suitable as a case rule.
The court held that once the plaintiff's title was admitted, defendants claiming tenancy bore the burden and had to begin.
The statement makes an overbroad res judicata rule and omits the different causes of action, non-participation, and limited effect of the earlier ex parte dismissal.
The title-investigation rule is correct, but the non-empty statute reference points to CPC section 114(2), which was construed for marked documents becoming part of the record.
